..
Issued at 228 AM MDT Sat Oct 24 2026

We are currently experiencing some rattling at the Riverton Weather 
Abode. This is coming compliments of our good friend cold advection, 
following the passage of a cold front. Some of the more prone areas, 
like near Buffalo, have seen wind gusts around 50 mph tonight. These 
events are usually short lived though, and most of the wind should 
be over by sunrise.

We are currently in a fast moving pattern, which will bring a few 
chances of precipitation to the area. The area will be in between 
systems today, which should bring a dry but cool start to the fourth 
weekend of the month, with temperatures averaging around 5 degrees 
below normal. The next chance of showers arrives tonight as the 
upper level low now located over Arizona that has been bringing all 
the severe weather to the desert southwest moves to the northeast. 
Thankfully, it will be significantly weaker when it arrives here 
tonight and Sunday. Recent model trends keep the low further east, 
taking it over southeastern Wyoming, and also keeping a bulk of the 
moisture east of the area. As a result, precipitation amounts should 
remain on the light side, with all locations except the Wind River 
Range having a less than 1 in 2 chance of a tenth of an inch or more 
of precipitation. Otherwise, expect a mostly cloudy and seasonable 
day. 

We should then have a period of quiet weather on Monday as there 
will be another gap in areas of low pressure. Then the second system 
arrives Monday night into Tuesday. This system is of Pacific origin 
and will have a bit moisture and jet energy to work with so impacts 
will be greater. However, with the flow zonal and rather fast, the 
low should be a fast mover to limit the duration of those impacts. 
As for the precipitation, most guidance shows the highest amounts 
across northern Wyoming, especially in the western mountains with a 
period of orographic enhancement. Most areas in the northwest have 
at least a 3 out of 4 chance of a tenth of an inch or more of QPF, 
with a 1 in 2 chance of a quarter of an inch or more. Due to the 
fast movement of the system, chances of a half an inch or more are 
generally less than 2 out of 5. The next question is how much will 
be snow. Some guidance shows 700 millibar temperatures falling as 
low as minus 6, which would lower snow levels to valley floors. The 
question is how much moisture will be left over when the cold air 
arrives. In the probabilistic realm of the ensembles. most of the 
mountains, as well as the Jackson Valley, have at least a 1 in 2 
chance of an inch or snow or more, with a similar chance of over 3 
inches above 8500 feet. However, due to the fast movement of the 
system, the chance of 6 inches is less than 1 out of 5, so 
advisories look unlikely at this time. Travel could be difficult for 
a time, since there will be an 100 knot jet over the area at the 
time, and there could be some blowing snow over the passes that 
could reduce visibility. 

And the strength of the jet, along with some strong southwest flow 
on the south side of the low, will bring strong wind to central and 
southern portions of the area on Tuesday. The NBM ensemble shows at 
least a 1 in 2 chance of wind gusts past 40 mph on Tuesday 
afternoon, with the area from Muddy Cap through Casper having at 
least 1 in 2 chance of gusts over 50 mph. The chance of gusts over 
60 mph is under 1 in 4 for the major travel corridors though, so 
wind highlights look unlikely at this point, but we will have to 
watch it closely. 

Quieter conditions should then move in for most of the remainder of 
the workweek with ridging building over the area, bring mainly dry 
conditions and above normal temperatures. A few orographic showers 
may occur across western Wyoming but it should be dry most of the 
time. A stronger system may approach for next weekend, but guidance 
diverges substantially this far out so details are very difficult to 
nail down this far out.
